greeting.text: Mara puts both hands flat on the bar. "You were paid to leave. You left. Don't stand in my doorway and expect a stool."
"Sit anywhere. Half the town's stopped coming in after dark. Habit, mostly. Nothing left out there to be frightened of."
"I've had two fights in here this week and both of them were about you." She fills a cup without being asked. "Sit at the end. The end's quieter."
Mara comes round the end of the bar. "Well?" she asks quietly. "Is he ill? That's one conversation. If he's drunk, that's another. I've been standing here for two days not knowing which it is."

choices.label: He's a bargeman off the river. He walked here and he stopped.
I'll pay for his bed and his supper.
Put him to work. He can fix that third step.
I'll walk him down to the boats.

greeting.text: "Corner table," Mara says, without looking over. "Still there. Still face down. I've checked his breathing twice from behind this bar, like a fool, and it's perfectly normal."

choices.label: I'll go and talk to him.
Why won't you wake him yourself?

greeting.text:
Mara sets both hands on the bar and leaves the cups alone for once.

"Say it slowly," she says.

choices.label: There's a stair under Granary Row and a road under your cellar wall.

greeting.text: "Behind the north wall, where the drain goes through. I've taken a lamp down there twice this week. I haven't put my arm in, and I'm not going to. That's what I'm paying you for."

Fresh mortar runs along the foot of the north wall. Mara's put a keg in front of it, though it doesn't hide much. "Eleven gold for the brick," she says. "Cheapest eleven gold I've ever spent. I haven't slept better in years." She wipes the bar. "A girl comes to the back door on Tuesdays now. She didn't used to have to."

"Nine in the lockup," Mara says. "Every one of them lives in a drain and was carrying somebody else's barley for a cut." She sets down the cloth. "The man who owns the hatch blames a former employee. Reed has to take the explanation. She's got nine people and a hatch, but no name to put to either."

choices.label: It was still the right thing.

greeting.text: The north wall is unchanged. Mara hasn't mentioned it since you told her. She's as warm as ever, though every so often she looks at that corner of the room a little too long.

choices.label: You don't have to like it.

greeting.text:
The third step no longer creaks. The man who was face down on the corner table a fortnight ago is working on kegs in the back. Mara's stopped counting down the week.

"He's up before me," she says. "I resent that, and I've decided to keep resenting it."

"My grain's gone up," Mara says. "Not the price. The man delivering it. Fourteen years with the same cart, and this week a different one. The new fellow wants paying on delivery and won't take the standing order." She looks at you. "I'm not asking what you've been doing. I'd only worry. But I've had to put a penny on the ale, and I'd rather you heard it from me than read it on the board."

"Somebody took the corner room," Mara says. "Paid for four nights, slept two, and asked about you. Not by name at first. He read out a list of things you'd done and asked which were true." She sets the glass down. "I told him I keep an inn. He said that was a good answer, then paid for the other two nights on his way out."

choices.label: Which ones did you say were true?

greeting.text: Mara comes round the bar and sets a cup at your usual table. "Sit," she says. "It's gone quiet out there, and I don't trust it. I'd rather tell you something myself before somebody downriver does."
"The Vance girl's in the lockup. Three days now." She wipes the same patch of bar. "Her father drank here for twenty years and never short-changed me."

choices.label: She was writing what she was told to write.
The rats were commuting. Something else was feeding them.
Dead. But there's a drain behind the north wall and something's using it.

greeting.text: "Room's four coppers, stew's two, and I've got nothing to say about anybody." She does not look up from the slate.

choices.label: There's a man asleep at your corner table.
The four sacks. Let me look at the north wall.

greeting.text: Mara has the slate out by the tap. "Twenty and the stew, then. Write it down if you tend to forget. There's a journal for that. It keeps better records than I do."
"Written it down? Good." Mara doesn't wait for an answer. "Tobin's on the market square. He owes me a lantern. You'll need light down there."

"Quiet." Mara listens to the floorboards. "Good. I lost a tally stick down there in the spring. If the rats left it, it'll be on the floor. Use the Search button to look properly, then Take what you find."

Mara takes the stick and runs her thumb over the notches. "Mine. I said it was from spring. Nobody listens." She puts it under the bar. "There's a draught in that cellar I can't track down. Cold on my ankles every night. Go back and Search again."
"A gap behind the north wall. Of course there is." Mara does not go to look. "That's for later, not tonight. Leave it be."
"You're bleeding on my floor." Mara points to the blood. "Room's on the house tonight. Sleep it off. On the road, when there's no roof, the Camp button does the same job."

choices.label: Thank you. I'll take the room.

greeting.text: You come back up with the drain grating under one arm. Mara looks at it, and then at you, and puts the cloth down for the first time all evening.

choices.label: The rats were commuting. Something else was feeding them.

greeting.text: "Well?" Mara has the coin ready in her fist and has clearly had it there for an hour.

choices.label: Dead. But there's a drain behind the north wall and something's using it.

greeting.text: "Four sacks I never bought, in my own cellar." She has not sat down since you came back up. "I've been trading with the granary since I was nineteen."

choices.label: Somebody used your cellar as a midden.
They didn't use the door at all. Let me look at the north wall.
There's a man asleep at your corner table.

greeting.text: "Cellar's quiet. Thank you for that." She slides a bowl across. "On the house until it isn't."

choices.label: There is a way into your cellar that isn't the stairs.

greeting.text: "Still down there, is it?" She nods toward the cellar. "The door's behind the tap. Mind the third step. It's been loose since spring, and I haven't had a week to fix it."

choices.label: There's a man asleep at your corner table.

greeting.text: Mara gives you a once-over. "First time in Rivermark? You've the look of it."

choices.label: Show me how things go here.

greeting.text: "Welcome to the Golden Flagon. Clean beds, hot stew, and a problem I'd pay to be rid of."

choices.label: There's a man asleep at your corner table.

cellar_terms.text: "Rats. Big ones, and too many for this time of year. They've got through four sacks of barley and a whole side of bacon. Kill them and I'll pay you twenty and feed you while you're in town."

choices.label: Rats don't turn up in numbers for nothing.

cellar_terms.text: "Rats. Big ones, and too many for this time of year. They've got through four sacks of barley and a whole side of bacon. Kill them and I'll pay you twenty and feed you while you're in town."

choices.label: Rats don't turn up in numbers for nothing.

she_shrugs.text: "They come for food. That's what rats do." She stops wiping. "But there are four sacks down there I didn't put there, if that's what you mean. I've been meaning to look for a fortnight."

interjections.text: Ilse, from the door: "Four sacks is a cart. Somebody drove that in."
Kessa, without turning round: "Rats. Grain. It's not a riddle."

choices.label: Who has a key to your cellar?

who_has_a_key.text: "Me. My girl, who's fourteen and afraid of the dark. And the granary, because they deliver." She pauses. "The granary delivers."

choices.label: Say nothing about this to anyone.

she_agrees.text: "I've run a public house for twenty-two years," Mara says. "I know how to not say a thing."

she_pays_up.text: Mara puts the coin on the bar. "Twenty, and the stew's yours while you're in town." She picks up the cloth. "I won't ask what was down there. I've a public house to run, and asking has cost me a fortnight before."

interjections.text: Ilse, on the way out: "There were four sacks of grain down there she did not buy. She knows. She has decided not to know."

the_sump.text: "Four sacks of barley gone to rot, stacked against the north wall, and a split hazel tally with them." You put the stick on the bar. Mara turns it over once. "That's the granary's mark," she says. "That's Hollis Marrow's own mark, on grain I never ordered, rotting in my cellar."

interjections.text: Aldric: "He was paid for it and could not deliver it, so he had to lose it somewhere that was not his own yard."
Kessa: "That's a lot of trouble to go to over barley." She turns the tally over once. "So it was never about the barley."

choices.label: Who has a key to your cellar?

the_grain_talk.text: "Hollis Marrow's people deliver here twice a month. I gave them a key to my hatch." She folds her arms. "Now you're going to ask me to say that in front of the watch."

choices.label: Just tell me what Marrow's been buying.
You've kept accounts thirty years. What does a granary reeve do with spoiled grain?
No. Keep it to yourself for now.

she_talks.text: "He buys the whole harvest forward, at a price set in spring, and sells it on through the year." She counts it off on the bar. "So a bad year makes him rich and a good year ruins him. And a road nobody can use makes him rich in a good year too."

interjections.text: Sera has gone very still by the door. "She's not wrong," she says, to nobody.
Aldric: "That is not gossip. That is arithmetic."

she_shuts_up.text: "No." Mara straightens. "I buried a husband and kept this roof up alone. I didn't do it by naming the man who sets the price of bread to a stranger with a sword. Four coppers for the room, two for the stew."

interjections.text: Kessa, quietly: "You pushed. She's got more to lose than you do."

she_is_frightened.text: "I am careful of him," Mara says. "There is a difference and you'll learn it if you stay in this town a season."

they_come_back.text: "They will," she agrees. "They always do. Then I'll pay somebody to kill them again, and that's the arrangement, and it's cheaper than finding out why."

about_town.text: "Old trade road. Quiet enough, until the raids." She glances at you. "I've heard you've been counting wagons. Carters talk in here, and they've noticed which ones get through."
"Rivermark sits on the old trade road. The quarry east of here fell in before you were born, and the town's argued about it ever since." She shrugs. "Now things live in it, and we're still arguing."

carters_blame.text: "Goblins, out loud. The granary, once they've had three." She takes the cup away. "You did not hear that from me and I will say so."

the_argument.text: "Reed wants it emptied. The council wants it left alone. Half the men who'd have to go down there dug it in the first place, and they won't go." She refills an unattended cup. "Meanwhile, something's been coming up out of it."

who_drinks_here.text: "The half-orc at the end of the bar has nursed the same cup since noon. She's paid for four. The cleric in the corner treats anyone who asks and won't take coin, so he's got a reason." She lowers her voice. "They're both waiting for something, but not the same thing."

the_warden.text: "There's a warden works the east hills. Thornwood. Comes in for salt about once a fortnight and goes out again before dark." Mara considers. "She's the only one in this town who goes toward the quarry on purpose."

sera_talk.text: "Maybe both," Mara says. "I've known her since she was small and she was never a liar. She was always a girl who did what she was told and hated it. That's a different fault and it hangs the same."

interjections.text: Aldric says nothing at all, and looks at the floor, and that is the loudest thing in the room.

after_steel.text: "It's not a complaint. Half my trade was carters who stopped here before taking the east road. Now they don't, because there's nothing to stop for." She shrugs. "You made us safe. Safe costs less than I thought."

interjections.text: Kessa: "Nobody thanks the wall for the wind it keeps off."

after_pact.text: "I'm on the side of whoever still buys ale." She sets the cloth down. "Which is currently both sides, so I'm doing better than the council. Ask me again in a year."

interjections.text: Ilse: "That is the most honest thing anyone in this town has said to us."

came_back.text: "About forty of us came back," Mara says. "The mill has no roof, and the granary burned with everything in it. We're still here. You're not staying."

the_corner_table.text:
"Two days," Mara says. "Two days at my corner table, in the seat by the fire, during market week."

She doesn't sound angry.

"He came in Monday, bought a small ale, drank a third, then put his head on his arms. That's all. He's not drunk. I've thrown out enough drunks to know the difference from across a room." She wipes the bar. "He's left four coppers on the table and hasn't touched them. He's showing me he won't steal. Every hour or so, he sits up, looks at the door, then puts his head down again."

interjections.text: Aldric, quietly: "He is waiting for somebody to come in. Or for himself to want to go out. I have done both of those in a room like this one."
Kessa: "Four coppers on the table where she can see them. That's a man with manners and nowhere to be."

choices.label: I'll wake him and find out what he needs.

why_not_wake_him.text:
"You learn young not to touch a sleeping man you haven't met," Mara says. "Last time I tried, it took six weeks for the tooth marks to heal. He was a perfectly nice fellow who'd been at sea."

She sets down the cloth.

"And if I go over there, I'm the landlady moving him on. He'll leave. I'd rather someone find out first whether he's got anywhere to go."

she_will_not.text: "No," Mara says. "I said I wanted him woken, fed, and paying or gone. I didn't say thrown out. Please hear the difference. I've chosen those words every morning since Monday."

choices.label: All right. I'll go and talk to him.

she_is_grateful.text: "Right." Mara finds something else to do with her hands. "There's stew in the pot. I haven't put it on his slate, and I'd rather nobody remarked on that."

corbin_the_truth.text:
Mara listens as you explain: nineteen years on the flat boats out of Greyhythe, then he stopped nine days ago and walked here. Uphill, he said. He wanted to be somewhere away from the water.

"Nineteen years," she says. "And he's got four coppers."

She looks toward the corner table.

"Right. Something has to happen. He can't sit in my fire seat all autumn, but I can't send him back on the road with four coppers and still recognise myself. So."

choices.label: I'll pay for his bed and his supper.
Put him to work. He can fix that third step.
I'll walk him down to the boats.

corbin_paid_for.text:
You pay ten coppers for a bed and a bowl. Mara gives him the bowl and doesn't mention it.

He sleeps eleven hours. On the second morning he comes down looking like a man again, eats everything in front of him, and asks Mara if there's work to do before he goes. He asks properly, standing up.

He takes the Thursday boat. After he's gone, a river man's knife is left on the bar, short and thick-backed, worn down from nineteen years of sharpening. That's a bargeman's whole toolkit. Leaving it behind means something.

interjections.text: Aldric turns the knife over once and puts it back down. "He will be all right," he says. "Not because of the bed. Because somebody paid for it in front of him."

corbin_works.text:
"A week," Mara says. "Pots, kegs, and that third step. Bed in the back and meals from the pot. If he's still here on the eighth day, we'll have to talk about it."

He fixes the step on the first morning, without being asked. Nobody at the Flagon has managed that since spring.

By the fourth day, Mara has stopped mentioning the week. Once, thinking the room is empty, he sings a long line, the sort you sing to keep time with a pole. Then he stops, embarrassed, and goes back to the kegs.

interjections.text: Kessa, from the end of the bar: "That's the first thing anyone's fixed in this town since we got here."
Ilse: "He needed a thing to do with his hands before anybody asked him a question. You got the order right."

corbin_walked_out.text:
You walk him down to the river stair and put him on a boat heading downriver. He asks for it after you ask him twice.

He says he's grateful and won't forget it. He means it until the boat casts off. That's no criticism. That's how the words work.

Mara gets her table back and wipes it twice.

interjections.text: Aldric watches the boat until it is round the bend, which takes some time, and does not say anything about it.

choices.label: Everyone got what they asked for.

he_is_staying.text: "He is not staying," says Mara. "He is here until the spring boats, and then he is going back on the water, and he has told me so twice." She stacks a mug. "He has also mended the yard gate, the shutter, and the pump, and none of those were the week, so we shall see."

the_north_wall.text:
Mara goes still.

"Say that again," she says.

You repeat it. Four sacks didn't come up the stairs behind the tap where she stands eighteen hours a day. They came through the wall, through the drain gap leading to the sump. That gap isn't natural. Someone has been removing a course of brick at a time and putting the loose ones back for years.

"I've stood on the other side of that wall since I was nineteen." Mara sets down the cloth and leaves it there. "Find out where it goes. I'll pay whatever it costs. I don't want to know the price."

interjections.text: Ilse: "A road, then. Not a nest. Roads have two ends and somebody maintains them."
Sera: "Grain that never crosses a weighing floor. Do you know what that is worth? Nobody does. That is the point of it."

choices.label: Brick it up and forget it.

she_gives_the_lamp.text:
"Take the good lamp," says Mara, "and take the long one off the hook by the door, because the good lamp will not last you and I would rather you had two than be brave about it."

She fills something for somebody without looking at either.

"And whatever is down there," she says, "it has been down there the whole time I have been up here. I should like that said out loud once before you go, because I have been telling myself for a fortnight that it is new."

choices.label: It has been down there the whole time.

not_yet.text: "I have thought about that every night for a fortnight," says Mara, "and every night I get as far as: and then I am a woman standing on a brick wall, not knowing." She picks the cloth back up after all. "Ask me again when I am tired enough."

the_route_explained.text:
You explain it slowly.

A brick stair under Granary Row leads to a loading hatch. The landing below has been swept cleaner than anywhere else under town. A dry conduit runs west from there, into half the cellars between the market and the quay, including Mara's.

The route bypasses the weighing floor. Nothing is tallied, taxed, or seen. Grain starts at the granary and disappears from the books.

"Four sacks in my cellar," Mara says.

"Four spoiled sacks," you say. "They weren't delivering to you. They were storing grain. Something went bad, and they left it there."

Mara sits on her own bar stool. You've never seen her do that.

interjections.text: Aldric: "How many cellars in this town have a north wall somebody has been taking apart a brick at a time?"
Kessa: "It's a warehouse. The whole under-side of this town is somebody's warehouse."

choices.label: Brick it. Your wall and the hatch, both.
There are sixty people down there who eat off that route.

sixty_people.text:
Mara takes a long time to answer.

"I know," she says. "I've known people lived down there since I was about thirty. A child came up from my cellar with a candle once. Neither of us screamed." She rubs her face. "I've left the hatch on the latch every winter since. Don't stand in my house and explain the sixty people to me."

She gets up.

"But it's not just sixty people now. It's sixty people and a *business*. One came first, and I want someone to tell me which one I'm protecting."

choices.label: Brick it. Your wall and the hatch, both.
Neither. Leave it open and I'll make my own arrangement.

she_bricks_it.text:
The work takes two days and eleven gold in brick. The mason is Mara's cousin's boy. Neither asks questions in front of the other.

The north wall is sealed. The hatch under Granary Row is a floor again.

Nothing comes down the grain stair or through the conduit. Much of what Undertown had been living on came that way. Nobody tells you while you're laying brick. You find out later, when fewer people come to the lamps.

she_calls_reed.text:
Reed posts four men at the hatch for a fortnight and arrests nine people at the bottom.

All nine live in the tunnels. They were carrying somebody else's barley for a cut, but none can name the owner. The arrangement was made with a man who came down twice a year with a slate and no name.

The granary books show nothing. They were never the point. The hatch's owner blames a former employee. It's a good explanation, and Reed writes it down.

"I've got nine people in my lockup who live in a drain," Captain Elowen Reed says. "I know exactly what I've caught, and what I haven't."

interjections.text: Ilse says nothing at all for the rest of the day, and camps well away from the fire that night.

the_tuesday_girl.text: "Somebody's," says Mara. "She is about nine and she comes up the area steps on a Tuesday and I give her what is going, and she says thank you and takes it back down." She wipes. "She used not to have to come to the door. That is all I am saying about it and it is more than I meant to."

was_it.text: "It was the lawful thing," says Mara, "and I have kept a public house for twenty-two years by knowing that those are two different words." She takes a cup away. "Nine of them. Not one name above them. And my north wall is still a hole, and next winter somebody will find another hatch, and we shall all do this again."

she_does_not.text:
"No," Mara agrees. "I do not." She fills something. "And I have not lost a sack since, and the girl comes to the door on a Tuesday, and every so often I stand at that end of the bar and think about how much of this town I do not know the underneath of."

She puts the cup down in front of you.

"Which is a thing I could have thought at any point in twenty-two years," she says, "and did not."

the_corner_room_man.text:
"He signed the book," Mara says. "Of course he did. Everyone signs, and I've never looked twice." She pulls it from under the tap and turns it around. The name is written neatly, but means nothing to either of you.

"As for which things were true, I told him I keep an inn. He wrote that down too, and didn't seem to mind. That's what stays with me. He wasn't fishing. He already knew. He wanted to see what I'd do."

after_the_survey.text: "Forty-one on the Row in the rain, and Reed wrote down every one," Mara says. "Half the town's been in since, asking what they're meant to do about it. The thing that wrote that figure is downriver, and Tull's packet goes down on the second and the fifth."

"I've swept a lot of ash in this inn and it has never once kept a secret," Mara says. "They'll start it all again, and then they'll go asking who stood by the fire. If you'd sooner be gone before the asking gets here, Tull's packet goes down on the second and the fifth."

Mara looks at your purse, and then at the paper beside it, and then at neither. "I'll not lecture anybody on taking money. I've taken worse for less," she says. "But a retainer's a leash with a pay-day, and whoever holds the other end will want you on Tull's packet. Second and the fifth."

"Word is you walked out of the works with a roll of paper nobody had thought to lock up," Mara says. "I won't ask what's in it. It's no use in my cellar, and from here it only goes one way: down the river on Tull's packet, the second and the fifth."

fn_rats_offer.text: Mara wipes the same patch of bar twice. "Rats. Big ones, and too many for this time of year. They've got through four sacks of barley and a side of bacon. Twenty to clear them out, and the stew's yours while you're in town."

fn_haggle_won.text: Mara considers the offer. "Twenty-five, then. And the stew. Don't tell the regulars. Write it down if you tend to forget. There's a journal for that. It keeps better records than I do."

fn_haggle_lost.text: "Twenty." Mara taps the slate. "And the stew. Write it down if you tend to forget. There's a journal for that. It keeps better records than I do."

fn_took_it.text: "Twenty, and the stew. Good." She nods toward the slate by the tap. "Write it down if you tend to forget. There's a journal for that. It keeps better records than I do."

fn_done.text: "That's the Flagon." Mara picks the cloth back up. "The rest of Rivermark is less forgiving."
